title: Bhagavad Gita, Chapter 6: training the mind
excerpt: An original meaning and contextual explanation of all 47 verses on meditation, steadiness, equal vision and devotion.
introHtml:
Chapter 6 develops the contemplative discipline introduced at the end of Chapter 5. Krishna describes preparation, posture, moderation and the repeated return of attention to the self. Arjuna then asks whether such steadiness is possible and what happens to someone who begins but falls short. The answer joins sustained effort with reassurance, ending in the image of a yogin whose inward life is devoted to Krishna.

Each Meaning gives an original English rendering of the displayed Sanskrit. Each Explanation follows the verse’s wording, its place in the dialogue and its philosophical or devotional context. These are original reader explanations; named traditional interpretations are identified where they are compared. [1–4]

verses.meaningHtml: The Lord said: One who performs the action that should be done without depending on its fruits is a renunciant and a yogin; merely giving up the sacred fire or ceasing activity does not make one so.
verses.explanationHtml: The sacred fire refers to the ritual responsibilities associated with a householder’s life. Giving it up can mark an outward change of religious condition, but Krishna makes freedom from dependence on fruits central to the present comparison. The verse carries Chapter 5’s account of inward renunciation into the discussion of meditation. The character of practice is established through what the person relinquishes in desire and identification.

verses.meaningHtml: What people call renunciation, know that to be yoga, Pandava; no one becomes a yogin without relinquishing desire-shaped intentions.
verses.explanationHtml: The key term saṅkalpa concerns the intentions and projections through which desired outcomes occupy the mind. Relinquishing their authority connects renunciation with the gathering of attention in yoga. Krishna thus identifies a shared inner condition before describing contemplative practice more fully. Meditation will require the same freedom from possessive expectation that earlier chapters associated with disciplined action.

verses.meaningHtml: For a contemplative who wishes to ascend to yoga, action is said to be the means. For that same person established in yoga, stillness is said to be the means.
verses.explanationHtml: The verse distinguishes preparation from establishment. Action can purify and train the person who is beginning, while śama, quieting or stillness, has a central role once concentration has matured. The reference to “that same person” shows a development within a life of practice. It helps explain why Krishna can commend active discipline and then turn to a setting of withdrawal and sustained contemplation.

verses.meaningHtml: When one is attached neither to sense objects nor to actions, and has relinquished desire-shaped intentions, one is said to be established in yoga.
verses.explanationHtml: The description includes attachment to activity itself as well as attachment to sensory objects. A person may loosen dependence on pleasures yet continue to define the self through being busy, successful or indispensable. Krishna locates establishment in a fuller release of such projections. This gives the stillness of 6.3 its inward meaning before the next verses examine the self’s capacity to support or undermine its own direction.

verses.meaningHtml: One should raise the self through the self and not let the self sink down. The self alone is the self’s friend, and the self alone is the self’s enemy.
verses.explanationHtml: The repeated ātman carries several related senses, including the person and the inner capacities through which the person can be governed. The verse turns attention toward that internal relationship. Habits of thought and response can either assist the movement toward clarity or repeatedly pull it away. Krishna therefore describes self-mastery as a matter of developing a supportive rather than adversarial relation within one’s own life.

verses.meaningHtml: For one who has mastered the self through the self, the self is a friend. But for one without self-mastery, the self behaves like an enemy.
verses.explanationHtml: This explains the contrast introduced in 6.5. Friendliness here means that inner capacities have become aligned with a considered purpose; hostility means that they repeatedly defeat it. The distinction concerns training and orientation rather than the existence of two separate persons inside the body. It prepares the chapter’s practical account of bringing mind, senses, intention and conduct into a steadier relationship.

verses.meaningHtml: For one who has mastered the self and is peaceful, the supreme self is steadily present amid cold and heat, pleasure and pain, honour and dishonour.
verses.explanationHtml: The paired experiences include bodily conditions, felt enjoyment and suffering, and social judgment. Steadiness is considered across all three. The reference to paramātman gives the description its spiritual centre: peace is joined with establishment in the highest self. The yogin’s condition is therefore shown through what remains stable as circumstances and the opinions of others change.

verses.meaningHtml: A yogin satisfied by knowledge and realised understanding, steady and master of the senses, is called disciplined, seeing a lump of earth, a stone and gold with equal regard.
verses.explanationHtml: Earth, stone and gold evoke sharply different worldly values. Equal regard indicates freedom from their power to determine the person’s inward condition. Knowledge has matured into a lived understanding that can remain steady in their presence. The verse links contemplation with the earlier account of contentment, showing that the training of mind changes what possession, comparison and valuation mean to the practitioner.

verses.meaningHtml: One whose understanding is even toward well-wishers, friends, enemies, the indifferent, mediators, those disliked, relatives, the good and wrongdoers is especially distinguished.
verses.explanationHtml: The range of relationships is deliberately broad. It includes those who help without expectation, close companions, opponents and people who stand between parties. Evenness concerns the understanding with which they are met, extending the equal vision of Chapter 5 into complicated human relations. The verse makes a social test of inward practice: steadiness must be able to survive more than favourable treatment.

verses.meaningHtml: A yogin should continually practise self-discipline in a secluded place, alone, with mind and self governed, free from expectation and possessive accumulation.
verses.explanationHtml: The chapter now turns to a particular setting for contemplation. Seclusion reduces competing demands, while the accompanying conditions address the desires and expectations a person could carry into solitude. Being alone is therefore part of a larger discipline of attention. Krishna describes the orientation in which the following preparations of seat, posture and gaze are to be understood.

verses.meaningHtml: In a clean place, one should establish a firm seat, neither too high nor too low, with cloth, a skin and kusha grass arranged for it.
verses.explanationHtml: The verse gives the contemplative setting a concrete material form. Cleanliness and a stable seat support sustained sitting, while the named materials belong to the practice world in which the passage was composed. Their order places cloth above the skin and grass. This careful preparation leads into the inward task described next: gathering the mind and governing the activities of the senses.

verses.meaningHtml: Seated there, making the mind one-pointed and governing the activities of mind and senses, one should practise yoga for inward purification.
verses.explanationHtml: The prepared seat is directed toward a specific purpose. Attention is gathered into ekāgratā, one-pointedness, while mental and sensory activity is brought under discipline. The aim of purification connects the practice with the action described in earlier chapters, where attachment and possessive identification were progressively loosened. Meditation belongs to that same transformation of the practitioner’s inner orientation.

verses.meaningHtml: Holding body, head and neck upright and steady, one should remain still, directing the gaze toward the tip of the nose and not looking around in different directions.
verses.explanationHtml: Bodily alignment and the direction of the gaze are described together as supports for steadiness. The instruction gathers attention instead of continually allowing new sights to redirect it. This develops the practical scene begun with the seat in 6.11. The next verse adds the ethical and devotional conditions of the practice, making clear how physical preparation belongs within a whole discipline.

verses.meaningHtml: Peaceful, free from fear and firm in the vow of celibate discipline, governing the mind and directing thought toward me, the yogin should sit with me as the highest aim.
verses.explanationHtml: The vow of brahmacarya gives the passage an ascetic context in which conduct supports contemplation. Peacefulness and freedom from fear accompany the mind’s direction toward Krishna. The phrase mat-para makes that orientation explicit: the practice is centred on him as its highest aim. Posture and concentration are therefore joined with a way of living and a devotional commitment.

verses.meaningHtml: Continually practising in this way, with the mind governed, the yogin attains peace whose culmination is liberation and whose foundation is in me.
verses.explanationHtml: The result is described as peace reaching its highest completion, grounded in Krishna. Repeated practice and the governance of mind remain part of the sentence, connecting that result with the preparation just given. The verse concludes this initial account of meditation before Krishna adds an important condition: the practitioner’s daily habits must also support the steadiness being sought.

verses.meaningHtml: Yoga is not for one who eats excessively, nor for one who does not eat at all, Arjuna; nor for one given to excessive sleep or continual wakefulness.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna considers the rhythm of embodied life alongside formal meditation. Extremes of eating and sleeping can work against the steadiness the practice requires. The verse’s paired structure makes balance central to the discussion. This continues the chapter’s insistence that contemplation depends on a whole way of living, preparing the positive account of measured habits in the next verse.

verses.meaningHtml: For one whose food and recreation are measured, whose effort in actions is measured, and whose sleep and waking are measured, yoga becomes a destroyer of suffering.
verses.explanationHtml: The repeated yukta suggests what is fitting, balanced or well ordered. Nourishment, recreation, work and rest are all brought within the scope of practice. Krishna thereby makes the conditions of contemplation continuous with everyday conduct. Yoga’s freeing effect is connected with a life whose different activities support one another, rather than repeatedly scattering the mind through incompatible demands.

verses.meaningHtml: When the thoroughly governed mind rests in the self alone, free from longing for all desired objects, a person is then said to be established in yoga.
verses.explanationHtml: The discussion moves from the conditions of practice to its inward character. The mind’s steadiness is located in the self, while craving no longer pulls it outward toward one imagined completion after another. This echoes the account of satisfaction in the self in 2.55. The following image of a lamp gives a visible form to the quality of attention being described.

verses.meaningHtml: A lamp standing in a windless place does not flicker: this is the comparison used for the yogin whose mind is governed while practising yoga of the self.
verses.explanationHtml: The flame remains luminous and steady when the currents that disturb it have quieted. The image describes the quality of attention associated with disciplined contemplation. Its force lies in stability rather than extinction: there is still light, but its motion no longer prevents steady illumination. The next verses elaborate what is disclosed when such gathered attention becomes established.

verses.meaningHtml: In that state the mind grows quiet, restrained through the practice of yoga; there, seeing the self through the self, one finds contentment in the self.
verses.explanationHtml: This begins a description continued through 6.23. Quieting the mind allows the self to become the focus of a different kind of seeing. Contentment arises within that recognition instead of depending on acquiring a new sensory object. The verse brings together the chapter’s practices of restraint with the earlier theme of inward fulfilment, explaining the point toward which the image of the steady flame was leading.

verses.meaningHtml: There one knows an ultimate happiness, grasped by understanding and beyond the senses; established in it, one does not depart from the truth.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna distinguishes this happiness through the capacity by which it is apprehended. It is beyond sensory enjoyment and is reached through a clarified understanding. The second clause stresses stability in what has been recognised. This continues the sequence begun in 6.20, where quieting mind, seeing the self and inward contentment are connected as aspects of an established contemplative condition.

verses.meaningHtml: Having attained that, one considers no other gain greater. Established in it, one is not shaken even by great suffering.
verses.explanationHtml: The description gives both a positive and a testing aspect of fulfilment. Nothing else appears capable of completing what has already been found, and severe adversity does not uproot that understanding. This develops the earlier contrast between inward happiness and dependence on changing contacts. The verse describes the ideal steadiness of the yogin as part of the passage’s account of the highest attainment.

verses.meaningHtml: Know that separation from association with suffering to be what is called yoga. This yoga should be practised with determination and a mind that does not lose heart.
verses.explanationHtml: The definition turns on viyoga, separation, within the word-world of yoga or joining. Release from the binding relationship with suffering gives the practice its purpose. Determination and the refusal to give way to despondency then bring the account back to effort. The verse connects the ideal just described with the repeated, patient work through which a practitioner approaches it.

verses.meaningHtml: Relinquishing completely all desires born from mental projections, one should govern the whole group of senses through the mind on every side.
verses.explanationHtml: Saṅkalpa again names the mental construction through which an imagined object becomes a projected source of completion. Krishna connects relinquishing such desires with governing the senses. The two are mutually relevant: sensory engagement can feed a projection, and a projection can direct the senses toward its object. This prepares the gradual settling of attention described in the next verse.

verses.meaningHtml: Little by little, one should become still through understanding held firm by resolve. Establishing the mind in the self, one should cease thinking of anything else.
verses.explanationHtml: The repeated “little by little” gives the practice a gradual rhythm. Understanding and firmness guide the mind’s settling rather than leaving it to follow each new projection. The final phrase is read within that movement of attention toward the self. It describes the contemplative direction being cultivated, which the next verse develops through the practical response to a mind that wanders.

verses.meaningHtml: Wherever the restless and unsteady mind moves away, one should bring it back from there and direct it into the governance of the self alone.
verses.explanationHtml: Wandering is treated as something encountered within practice. The instruction therefore provides a repeated response: notice the direction of movement and return attention to its settled centre. It follows the gradual approach in 6.25 and gives perseverance a concrete form. The mind’s instability does not end the inquiry; working with that instability becomes part of the discipline itself.

verses.meaningHtml: The highest happiness comes to this yogin whose mind is peaceful, whose passion has quieted, who is free from stain and established in Brahman.
verses.explanationHtml: The quieting of rajas links meditation with the account of nature’s qualities in earlier chapters. Restlessness and the pressure of acquisition have become calm, allowing the happiness associated with Brahman to be described as coming to the practitioner. The verse gathers mental peace, purification and spiritual understanding into one condition, rather than treating concentration as an isolated accomplishment.

verses.meaningHtml: Continually practising in this way, the yogin whose faults have fallen away readily experiences the limitless happiness of contact with Brahman.
verses.explanationHtml: The expression brahma-saṃsparśa gives a language of contact to an attainment earlier described as beyond sensory objects. Here it concerns the relationship to Brahman, rather than ordinary sense contact. Continuing practice and purification remain part of the account. The following verses show how this inward recognition expands into the way all beings and their relation to Krishna are seen.

verses.meaningHtml: The self joined to yoga, looking everywhere with equal vision, sees the self present in all beings and all beings present in the self.
verses.explanationHtml: The scope of contemplative vision now becomes universal. Traditional interpretations differ over its metaphysics: Shankara reads the passage through the identity of self and Brahman, while Ramanuja emphasises the essential likeness of selves apart from their embodied differences. The immediate movement is toward equal vision across beings, extending the equality described in Chapter 5. [3]

verses.meaningHtml: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me never loses sight of me, and I never lose sight of that person.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna now speaks personally within the universal vision described in 6.29. Seeing him in all things and all things in him establishes a relationship that is no longer confined to one place or occasion. The paired assurance makes that relation reciprocal. The verse carries contemplation into a continuing recognition of divine presence within the world in which the yogin lives.

verses.meaningHtml: The yogin who worships me as present in all beings, established in unity, abides in me however that person may live and act.
verses.explanationHtml: The verse joins worship, unity and the recognition of Krishna in beings. Its final clause extends abiding in him across the circumstances of life, carrying the insight beyond the secluded meditation setting. This continues the Gita’s repeated connection between realised understanding and action. The following verse makes the implications for another being’s happiness and suffering especially direct.

verses.meaningHtml: One who sees happiness and suffering everywhere with equal regard by comparison with the self is considered by me the highest yogin, Arjuna.
verses.explanationHtml: Ātmaupamya, comparison with oneself, gives the teaching an immediately intelligible ethical form. Another being’s happiness and suffering are considered with the seriousness one gives to one’s own. This develops equal vision into a capacity to recognise the significance of others’ experience. The verse thus connects the deepest contemplative account with the relationships in which the practitioner’s understanding must become visible.

verses.meaningHtml: Arjuna said: Madhusudana, I do not see how the yoga you have described through evenness can remain firmly established, because the mind is so restless.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna’s objection turns the account of ideal steadiness toward the difficulty of actual practice. He understands the importance of evenness but cannot yet see how the mind can sustain it. The question gives an ordinary obstacle a central place in the dialogue. Krishna must respond to the conditions under which someone begins the path, rather than merely repeat its completed ideal.

verses.meaningHtml: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and obstinate. I consider governing it as difficult as governing the wind.
verses.explanationHtml: The accumulating descriptions give Arjuna’s difficulty weight. Mind changes direction, disrupts intentions, exerts force and persists in its habits. The wind image conveys something that seems to escape the person trying to contain it. This is a practical objection to the possibility of sustained contemplation, and Krishna’s response begins by accepting the reality of the difficulty.

verses.meaningHtml: The Lord said: Without doubt, mighty-armed one, the mind is restless and difficult to govern. But it is brought under discipline through repeated practice and dispassion, son of Kunti.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna answers with agreement before identifying two complementary means. Abhyāsa is repeated practice, while vairāgya concerns loosening attachment to what pulls attention away. One develops the capacity to return; the other reduces the force of the competing demand. Together they make the account of discipline more precise, connecting the repeated return in 6.26 with the relinquishment described earlier in the chapter.

verses.meaningHtml: In my view, yoga is difficult to attain for one without self-restraint. But a self-governed person who strives can attain it through an appropriate means.
verses.explanationHtml: The difficulty is stated alongside the possibility of attainment. The verse places effort within a workable method, continuing the paired disciplines of practice and dispassion. Self-governance also joins this answer to the chapter’s opening contrast between the self as friend and as enemy. Arjuna’s objection therefore receives a path of development rather than a demand that the mind already possess perfect stability.

verses.meaningHtml: Arjuna said: What becomes of someone who has trust but insufficient perseverance, whose mind falls away from yoga before attaining its perfection, Krishna?
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna now asks about an incomplete undertaking. The person he imagines is sincere enough to begin with śraddhā, yet does not sustain the practice to completion. The question is therefore different from deliberate refusal to engage. It brings the risk of failure into the conversation and asks whether beginning a demanding spiritual path can leave a person worse off if the goal is not reached.

verses.meaningHtml: Does such a person, fallen away from both ways, perish like a torn cloud, without a firm support and bewildered on the path to Brahman, mighty-armed one?
verses.explanationHtml: The torn cloud supplies an image of losing coherence and support. “Both ways” expresses Arjuna’s fear that someone may have loosened attachment to ordinary rewards without attaining the fulfilment promised by yoga. This is a serious objection to undertaking the path at all. The following assurance therefore addresses the continuity and value of sincere effort even when its immediate outcome is incomplete.

verses.meaningHtml: Krishna, you should remove this doubt of mine completely, for no one other than you is able to resolve it.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna asks for a full answer to the particular doubt raised in 6.37–38. His reliance on Krishna reflects the speaker’s claim to knowledge reaching beyond the present life. The request also shows how inquiry functions within their relationship: Arjuna does not conceal his difficulty, but makes it the object of instruction. Krishna’s answer will begin with reassurance before describing the seeker’s future course.

verses.meaningHtml: The Lord said: Partha, there is no destruction for that person either here or hereafter. No one who does what is good goes toward an evil destiny, dear one.
verses.explanationHtml: The assurance answers the fear of the torn cloud directly. Sincere beneficial effort is not presented as becoming worthless because the highest attainment was not completed in one life. Krishna’s affectionate address also changes the tone from severity to reassurance. Within the Gita’s account of continuing existence, the following verses explain how the unfinished work can receive further conditions for development.

verses.meaningHtml: Having reached the worlds of those who act meritoriously and lived there for long ages, the one who fell short in yoga is born into a pure and prosperous household.
verses.explanationHtml: The answer is framed within the text’s teaching of worlds, merit and rebirth. The seeker first receives the fruit of beneficial conduct, then gains circumstances favourable to further development. Purity and prosperity describe the household named in this account. The emphasis falls on continuity: an incomplete attempt at yoga has consequences that support a future opportunity rather than ending in the total loss Arjuna feared.

verses.meaningHtml: Or such a person is born into a family of wise yogins. A birth of this kind is even more difficult to obtain in the world.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna offers another favourable setting for renewed practice: a household where the discipline and its understanding are already present. Its rarity highlights the value of circumstances that make spiritual learning more readily available. This continues the explanation of how an unfinished path can be resumed. The verse’s focus is the opportunity for development provided by that setting.

verses.meaningHtml: There the person regains the connection with understanding developed in the previous body and strives again toward perfection, descendant of Kuru.
verses.explanationHtml: The earlier practice is described as leaving a continuity of understanding beyond one embodied life. In the new setting, that connection becomes available again and gives renewed effort its direction. Krishna’s account therefore addresses both preparation and agency: favourable circumstances matter, and the person also resumes striving. The next verse explains how strongly earlier practice can draw the seeker onward.

verses.meaningHtml: Through that earlier practice, the person is carried forward even without full control. Even one who seeks to know yoga goes beyond the domain of the sacred word.
verses.explanationHtml: The momentum of previous effort is described as continuing to work within the seeker. Śabda-brahman, the sacred word, here names the sphere of revealed verbal teaching and its prescribed observances. The movement beyond it concerns the realisation toward which practice tends. This develops the chapter’s assurance that sincere effort has an enduring direction, even before the highest fulfilment has been reached.

verses.meaningHtml: But the yogin who strives earnestly, purified of faults and brought to maturity through many births, then reaches the highest destination.
verses.explanationHtml: The answer combines long development with present exertion. Earlier practice supplies continuity, while purification and renewed effort remain necessary to the account. “Many births” places attainment within a horizon larger than one visible attempt. The verse completes Krishna’s response to the fear of failure by describing an unfinished path as capable of reaching fulfilment through sustained maturation.

verses.meaningHtml: The yogin is higher than practitioners of austerity, is considered higher than possessors of knowledge, and is higher than performers of ritual action. Therefore become a yogin, Arjuna.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna praises yoga by comparison with several recognised disciplines. Commentators specify the knowledge being compared: Shankara identifies scriptural learning here, while Ramanuja describes knowledge other than knowledge of the self. The comparison therefore brings the stress onto the realised understanding developed in the chapter. Its purpose is to encourage Arjuna toward the practice whose preparation and fulfilment have just been explained. [4]

verses.meaningHtml: And among all yogins, the one who worships me with trust, with the inward self absorbed in me, is considered by me the most deeply joined in yoga.
verses.explanationHtml: The chapter closes by giving its highest description a devotional centre. The inward absorption developed through meditation is directed toward Krishna and expressed in trusting worship. This recalls the instruction to sit with him as the highest aim in 6.14 and the universal vision of 6.30–31. It also opens naturally into Chapter 7, where Krishna explains more fully how he is to be known.
